quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: The '-ed' ending on the verb signals this already happened.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + past verb (called) + object (the clinic) + time (yesterday morning). Regular past tense verbs add '-ed' to show a completed action.
quests.textToSpeak: I called the clinic yesterday morning.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'About the leak' explains the subject of the message, coming last.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + past verb (emailed) + object (the landlord) + topic (about the leak). 'About' introduces what the communication concerns.
quests.textToSpeak: She emailed the landlord about the leak.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Together' closes the sentence, describing how the group moved.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + past verb (walked) + place (to the station) + manner (together). 'To' shows the direction of movement toward a destination.
quests.textToSpeak: We walked to the station together.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Forgot' doesn't follow the '-ed' pattern — it's an irregular past form you simply have to know.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + irregular past (forgot) + object (his umbrella) + place (at the cafe). 'Forgot' is the irregular past tense of 'forget'.
quests.textToSpeak: He forgot his umbrella at the cafe.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Found' is the irregular past of 'find' — listen for that short vowel change.
quests.explanation: Subject (They) + irregular past (found) + adjective + noun (a great apartment) + place (downtown). Irregular verbs change form rather than adding '-ed'.
quests.textToSpeak: They found a great apartment downtown.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Left' sounds nothing like 'leave' — irregular verbs often shift completely.
quests.explanation: Subject (I) + irregular past (left) + object (my phone charger) + place (at home). 'Left' is the irregular past tense of 'leave'.
quests.textToSpeak: I left my phone charger at home.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Didn't' carries the negative, so the main verb returns to its base form.
quests.explanation: Subject (She) + 'didn't' + base verb (answer) + object (my last message). After 'didn't', the main verb drops its past-tense ending.
quests.textToSpeak: She didn't answer my last message.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Such a' intensifies the noun phrase that follows it.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'didn't' + base verb (expect) + intensifier (such a) + adjective + noun (big crowd). 'Such a' adds emphasis before an adjective and noun.
quests.textToSpeak: We didn't expect such a big crowd.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'On time' means by the expected deadline, closing the sentence.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + 'didn't' + base verb (finish) + object (the assignment) + 'on time'. 'On time' means exactly when expected, neither early nor late.
quests.textToSpeak: He didn't finish the assignment on time.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Did' leads the question, and the main verb after it stays in base form.
quests.explanation: 'Did' + subject (you) + base verb (lock) + object (the front door)? Past tense questions move 'did' to the front and simplify the main verb.
quests.textToSpeak: Did you lock the front door?

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'When' asks for the time, and 'did' follows right behind it before the subject.
quests.explanation: 'When' + 'did' + subject (the delivery) + base verb (arrive)? Wh-questions in the past still need 'did' plus the base verb.
quests.textToSpeak: When did the delivery arrive?

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Late' at the end answers what went differently than expected.
quests.explanation: 'Why' + 'did' + subject (the meeting) + base verb (start) + adverb (late)? 'Late' describes the unexpected timing being questioned.
quests.textToSpeak: Why did the meeting start late?

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'I'm going to' announces a plan already decided, not a spontaneous idea.
quests.explanation: 'I'm' (I am) + 'going to' + verb (visit) + object (my cousin) + time (next week). 'Going to' expresses a plan made before the moment of speaking.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm going to visit my cousin next week.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'They're' contracts smoothly into the sentence before the plan itself.
quests.explanation: 'They're' (They are) + 'going to' + verb (renovate) + object (the kitchen) + time (soon). The contraction keeps the sentence flowing naturally when spoken.
quests.textToSpeak: They're going to renovate the kitchen soon.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'For that job' names the target of the application, coming last.
quests.explanation: 'She's' (She is) + 'going to' + verb (apply) + 'for that job'. 'Apply for' is a fixed pairing — you always apply 'for' something.
quests.textToSpeak: She's going to apply for that job.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Will' predicts something without personal certainty, unlike a fixed plan.
quests.explanation: Subject (The prices) + 'will' + base verb (rise) + time (next month). 'Will' is used for predictions based on general expectation.
quests.textToSpeak: The prices will rise next month.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: This isn't a prediction — it's a promise made right at the moment of speaking.
quests.explanation: 'I'll' (I will) + verb (help) + object (you) + verb 2 (carry) + object 2 (those boxes). Promises made on the spot often use 'will', contracted as 'I'll'.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll help you carry those boxes.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Won't' contracts 'will not' — and 'until' marks the point things might change.
quests.explanation: Subject (It) + 'won't' (will + not) + base verb (rain) + 'until the evening'. 'Until' shows a boundary in time that the negative prediction holds up to.
quests.textToSpeak: It won't rain until the evening.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Than' always follows a comparative adjective — listen for that pairing.
quests.explanation: Subject (This route) + verb (is) + comparative (shorter) + 'than' + comparison (the highway). Short adjectives add '-er' and pair with 'than'.
quests.textToSpeak: This route is shorter than the highway.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Mine' replaces 'my phone' — a possessive pronoun standing in for a full noun phrase.
quests.explanation: Subject (Her new phone) + verb (is) + comparative (faster) + 'than' + possessive pronoun (mine). 'Mine' avoids repeating 'my phone' a second time.
quests.textToSpeak: Her new phone is faster than mine.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'Better' is an irregular comparative — it doesn't follow the usual '-er' pattern.
quests.explanation: Subject (The second interview) + verb (went) + comparative (better) + 'than' + comparison (the first). 'Better' is the irregular comparative form of 'good' or 'well'.
quests.textToSpeak: The second interview went better than the first.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'Enough' follows the noun quantity it measures, unlike 'many' which comes before.
quests.explanation: Subject (We) + 'don't have' + quantifier (enough) + noun (chairs) + 'for everyone'. 'Enough' can follow a noun to show insufficient quantity.
quests.textToSpeak: We don't have enough chairs for everyone.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Too much' warns of excess — it sits directly before the noun it measures.
quests.explanation: Subject (He) + verb (spends) + quantifier (too much) + noun (time) + place (online). 'Too much' pairs with uncountable nouns like 'time'.
quests.textToSpeak: He spends too much time online.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'A lot of' is a longer quantity phrase, but it still acts like one unit before the noun.
quests.explanation: 'There's' (There is) + quantifier (a lot of) + noun (traffic) + time (this morning). 'A lot of' works with both countable and uncountable nouns.
quests.textToSpeak: There's a lot of traffic this morning.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: 'When' introduces a future condition — the call depends on that moment.
quests.explanation: Verb (Call) + object (me) + 'when' + time clause (you reach the airport). 'When' links an instruction to the future moment that triggers it.
quests.textToSpeak: Call me when you reach the airport.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: 'Before' places the locking action ahead of the leaving — even though 'leave' is mentioned last.
quests.explanation: Verb (Lock) + object (the door) + 'before' + time clause (you leave). The first action mentioned isn't always the one 'before' refers to.
quests.textToSpeak: Lock the door before you leave.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: 'After' points to something that hasn't happened yet, but will come first in time.
quests.explanation: 'We'll' (We will) + verb (talk) + degree (more) + 'after' + time reference (the presentation). 'After' shows the talk depends on the earlier event finishing.
quests.textToSpeak: We'll talk more after the presentation.

quests.instruction: Snap the scrambled words back into the order you hear.
quests.hint: Past tense opens the sentence, then 'but' flips it into a future promise.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (Sales were lower last quarter) + 'but' + clause 2 (they'll improve soon). Past fact and future prediction can sit side by side, contrasted by 'but'.
quests.textToSpeak: Sales were lower last quarter, but they'll improve soon.

quests.instruction: Listen closely, then rebuild the sentence in the order you hear it.
quests.hint: Both halves are in the past, but 'before' shows which one happened first.
quests.explanation: Clause 1 (I booked the flight) + 'before' + clause 2 (the prices went up). Even with two past actions, 'before' clarifies their real sequence.
quests.textToSpeak: I booked the flight before the prices went up.

quests.instruction: Put the scrambled words back in the order you hear them.
quests.hint: Two comparisons appear back to back, joined by 'but' — listen for the shift in feeling between them.
quests.explanation: Comparison 1 (stricter than the last one) + 'but' + comparison 2 (fairer overall). Two comparatives can balance a mixed opinion about the same subject.
quests.textToSpeak: The new manager is stricter than the last one, but fairer overall.
